analysis.one_liner: Makes war profiteering a federal crime, tightens competition rules for federal contracts, and restricts the revolving door.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 30 Senate cosponsors, the bill never received so much as a committee vote and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would criminalize war profiteering, with prison terms up to 20 years and fines up to twice a contractor's profits. It would bar companies that repeatedly overcharge the government from getting new contracts, require real competition on large contract awards, publish contractors' fines and violations on a public website, block companies from being paid both to help award contracts and to perform the work they oversee, and extend the ban on officials taking contractor jobs from one year to two years. It also strengthens protections for federal employees who report waste and fraud.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who ultimately pay for overpriced and sole-source federal contracts, especially in defense. Federal employees who expose waste, fraud, or abuse would gain stronger protection against retaliation. Smaller contractors would gain a fairer chance to compete for work now funneled to incumbent firms.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new federal crime of war profiteering and fraud, punishable by up to 20 years in prison and a fine of the greater of $1 million or twice the profits gained from the offense, with asset forfeiture and money-laundering treatment.

Revises federal acquisition rules so a company with a pattern of overcharging the government or violating tax, labor, environmental, antitrust, or consumer protection laws no longer qualifies as having a satisfactory record of integrity, allowing its suspension or debarment.

Bars monopoly-style single-award contract vehicles worth over $100 million unless an agency head gives a written public-interest justification, and requires competition for individual purchases over $1 million made under multiple-award contracts, with restored protest rights above $500,000.

Prohibits agencies from hiring contractors to perform inherently governmental functions or to help award and manage contracts they have a financial stake in, and bars former contractor employees from working on procurements involving their former employer for two years.
Publishes contractor fines, penalties, settlements, and guilty pleas, plus all sole-source awards over $2 million, on a publicly available federal procurement website.

Expands whistleblower protections, letting federal employees credibly report waste, abuse, and gross mismanagement without restriction on time, place, or form, and protecting classified disclosures of evidence of wrongdoing made to authorized members of Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Large federal and defense contractors, which would face new criminal liability, fines tied to profits, possible debarment for repeated overcharging, mandatory competition on large orders, and published records of their penalties. Federal agencies would also bear the cost of running more competitive procurements and keeping more functions in-house.

drawbacks.text: Requiring competition on individual orders over $1 million and stricter conflict-of-interest rules could slow procurement and raise administrative costs, a real concern for agencies that need to buy quickly during emergencies or military operations.

Prohibiting contracts for functions 'closely associated with inherently governmental functions' could force agencies to hire more in-house staff for planning and oversight work, shifting work from the private sector to the federal payroll.

The minimum-credential requirements for political appointees in contracting and safety jobs are stated in broad terms like 'superior record of achievement,' leaving room for officials to apply them inconsistently.

Broader whistleblower protections, including for classified information disclosed to Congress, would raise the volume of internal disclosures agencies must review and could generate disputes over what counts as a protected report.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a concrete taxpayer problem: paying private companies for government work, including war-zone work, with limited competition and weak penalties for overcharging. Its costs are administrative — slower procurements, more compliance, and more in-house staff — which are modest against fines that can reach twice a contractor's profits from fraud. The main weakness is design detail: the broad credentials test for appointees and the sweeping 'closely associated' functions ban would have needed careful implementation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Byron Dorgan and 28 listed colleagues introduced the bill in the Senate on March 2, 2006, and it was read twice and referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the same day.
Thirty senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill.
The only further actions in the record are two rounds of sponsor introductory remarks, on March 3 and July 27, 2006; the committee never reported the bill and the Senate never voted on it.
The bill died with the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007, without a committee markup or floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large federal and defense contractors are better off, since they keep the existing contracting system with no new criminal penalties, no mandatory competition on large orders, and no published record of their fines and violations. Taxpayers continue to bear the cost of the overcharging and sole-source awards the bill targeted.

for.name: Sen. Byron Dorgan
for.role: U.S. Senator from North Dakota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 2, 2006 and delivered sponsor remarks on the floor in March and July 2006.

for.name: 30 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a caucus-scale bloc of support that never produced committee action.

against.name: Sen. Susan Collins
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; the record shows referral and sponsor remarks only, with no markup, hearing, or committee vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican support appears in the record; Republicans held the Senate majority and controlled the committee to which the bill was referred, and the bill received no committee or floor action.

industries.note: The bill would create a war-profiteering crime with fines up to twice a company's profits, let agencies debar firms with a pattern of overcharging, and require competition on large contract vehicles. These companies sell to the government, so every dollar of overcharging comes out of taxpayers' pockets.

The bill would bar agencies from hiring contractors for inherently governmental functions and for contract-award oversight work, cutting into the business of firms that staff government management functions — including firms that currently help decide who gets contracts and also perform the work.
Mandatory competition on large multiple-award orders and restored protest rights above $500,000 would give smaller firms a fair shot at work now concentrated among incumbents.
